title: Classification & Routing
summary:
**Product:** a model that labels a request (intent, risk level, queue, which model or workflow handles it) and the system acts on the label. Because a *label* is the output, evaluation is **reference-based**: a human-labelled set, scored automatically. An LLM judge is only for ambiguous labels, not the default.

**What to measure**
- **Per-class precision and recall**, and the **confusion matrix**. Overall accuracy is dominated by common classes and can hide a failing rare, high-risk class.
- **Macro-F1** (every class counts equally) next to micro/weighted-F1 (frequency weighted).
- **Cost-weighted errors**: a missed fraud case and an unnecessary expensive workflow cost different amounts.
- **Calibration** (ECE, Brier): is confidence usable as a threshold?
- **Abstention and out-of-distribution (OOD)**: unknown intents should reach a fallback, not be forced into the nearest class.
- **Stability** under paraphrase, typos, languages, and prompt-injected text.

**Failure modes:** majority-class collapse, confidently wrong routing, label drift, forced classification of unknown inputs, injected text that steers the route.

**Choosing metrics:** gate high-risk classes on their own recall (and precision for costly routes), then report coverage vs accuracy at the confidence threshold. Evaluate on both a balanced set and the real production distribution. Compare with [structured extraction](#/sd/f/eval-structured-extraction) (fields instead of one label).

drills.q: Binary route "fraud review" on 1,000 requests. Confusion matrix for the fraud class: TP = 45, FN = 15, FP = 30, TN = 910. What is the F1 score of the fraud class, to two decimals?
drills.explain: Precision = 45/75 = 0.60, recall = 45/60 = 0.75, F1 = 2 x 0.6 x 0.75 / 1.35 = 0.667. Accuracy would be (45+910)/1000 = 95.5%, which looks great and hides that a quarter of fraud is missed.

drills.q: A router has two classes in a 1,000-example test set. Class A (900 examples) has F1 = 0.90 and class B (100 examples) has F1 = 0.50. What is the macro-F1?
drills.explain: Macro averages classes equally: (0.90 + 0.50) / 2 = 0.70. The frequency-weighted F1 would be (0.9x900 + 0.5x100)/1000 = 0.86, which hides class B's weakness.

drills.q: A "high-risk" class makes up 1% of traffic. A router that always predicts "normal" scores 99% accuracy. What should the release gate use instead?
options: Accuracy, but on a larger test set
Overall F1 computed with micro averaging
Per-class recall (and precision) of the high-risk class, with a hard threshold, plus the confusion matrix
drills.explain: Accuracy and micro-F1 are dominated by the majority class. The business question is how many high-risk cases are caught and how many ordinary requests are wrongly escalated.

drills.q: At a confidence threshold of 0.85, the router auto-handles 600 of 1,000 test requests and 582 of those are routed correctly; the other 400 go to a human fallback. What is the accuracy on the auto-handled requests (selective accuracy), in percent?
drills.explain: 582 / 600 = 97%, at 60% coverage. Raising the threshold usually increases selective accuracy and lowers coverage; pick the point where the human fallback cost balances the cost of errors.

drills.q: Users sometimes ask things your taxonomy does not contain ("how do I delete my cat"). How should this be evaluated?
options: Ignore them; the taxonomy defines the product
Include a labelled out-of-distribution slice and measure how often the router abstains or falls back instead of picking a confident wrong class
Have an LLM judge decide whether the nearest class is good enough
drills.explain: Forced classification turns unknowns into confident errors. Measure OOD recall (unknown correctly sent to fallback) together with the false-abstain rate on in-scope requests.

drills.q: How do you measure a classification or routing model, and why is a judge usually the wrong tool?
drills.answer: Use a labelled reference set and score automatically: per-class precision/recall, confusion matrix, macro- and weighted-F1, cost-weighted errors, calibration, abstention and OOD recall, paraphrase stability. A label is objective given a gold set, so an LLM judge adds cost and noise; use judges or human adjudication only to resolve ambiguous labels when building the gold set. Gate high-risk classes separately rather than on overall accuracy.
